sections.h2: What are the quickest ways to sell in Brick Township?
sections.html:
A seller in Brick has three realistic paths: hire an agent, handle the sale alone, or sign with a cash buyer who purchases the property untouched. Cash moves fastest and generally pays least. Listing adds commission and fix-up costs and takes longer. The right choice turns on the roof, the flood history, your deadline, and what the house would net after each route.

Ocean County's Brick Township was estimated at 77,402 people in mid-2025, up 5.1% from the 2020 base, per the Census Bureau. That growth, in a place that lost population between 2000 and 2020, means buyers are active, but the housing stock is mostly decades old. Many sellers meet the same questions: flood zones, inspection paperwork, and quarterly tax bills.

sections.h2: What kind of housing market is Brick Township?
sections.html:
Brick is a mature shore suburb where owners dominate. The 2020-2024 survey counts 30,289 households, 82.2% of them owning, with a $410,600 median home value and $106,130 median income. Rent runs $1,756 a month at the median, so a rental is a realistic fallback for some owners but not a cheap one to maintain under the township's inspection rules.

The township covers 25.59 square miles of land plus a lot of water. The mainland sits along the Metedeconk River and Barnegat Bay, and a separate set of ocean beaches (Brick Ocean Beaches I, II and III) lies on the barrier peninsula. Because the two parts do not touch, a street address can mean very different insurance and elevation questions. Older neighborhoods such as Laurelton, Lake Riviera and Baywood grew after the Garden State Parkway opened in 1954 and a building boom ran through the 1980s.

  • Many homes date from the 1950s through the 1980s, so roofs, septic or sewer connections, and electrical panels are common negotiation points.
  • Waterfront and bayfront lots near Cherry Quay, Havens Cove and Shore Acres carry their own flood and elevation questions.
  • Herbertsville and Parkway Pines sit near Parkway exit 91, away from the rest of the township, and attract commuters.

sections.h2: How does flood risk change a Brick home sale?
sections.html:
Flood history is the single biggest local variable. Hurricane Sandy in October 2012 devastated parts of Brick, and barrier island and waterfront properties took the worst of it; some buildings had to be torn down. A February 2026 blizzard also dropped roughly two feet of snow and knocked out power in several areas, which is a reminder that roofs and heating systems matter even away from the water.

The township's floodplain information page says it provides flood zone data to realtors, lenders, insurers and owners, including base flood elevation, whether a lot is in a coastal barrier area, and whether flood insurance is mandatory. Elevation certificates on file can be searched through the township's mapping tool, or requested from the engineering office by address or block and lot. Pull the certificate before you list, because a buyer's lender will ask for it.

Brick takes part in the federal Community Rating System, which can lower flood premiums. Its floodplain plan lists 140 mitigation initiatives, 81 of them completed by the latest annual report. A seller who can show an elevation certificate, a recent flood policy, and any raised-utility work usually faces fewer price cuts.

sections.h2: Which schools and roads do Brick buyers ask about?
sections.html:
Brick Public Schools serves pre-kindergarten through grade 12 inside the township. The district ran 12 schools and about 8,414 students in 2020-21, with elementary schools such as Drum Point, Lanes Mill, Midstreams, Osbornville, Veterans Memorial and Emma Havens Young, two middle schools (Lake Riviera and Veterans Memorial), and two high schools: Brick Memorial and Brick Township High School. Buyers often check which elementary zone a street falls in, so mention it in the listing.

The Garden State Parkway crosses the western side with exits 89, 90 and 91. Routes 70, 88 and 35 and county routes 528 and 549 handle local traffic. The old Laurelton Circle at Routes 70 and 88 once carried about 95,000 vehicles a day before it became a signal-controlled intersection in 1986. NJ Transit runs the 137 bus to the Port Authority Bus Terminal in Manhattan and the 67 to Newark, and a Park and Ride at exit 91 serves express commuters. Average commute time for workers is 28.2 minutes.

sections.h2: What township paperwork applies when a Brick house is sold or rented?
sections.html:
Brick's Division of Inspections, which is the Building Department, issues construction permits and handles requests for certificates under the New Jersey Uniform Construction Code. Open or unclosed permits are the usual cause of delay at closing, so have the division confirm the status of past work before you sign. The building office answers permit and certificate questions by voicemail and email, listed in the table below.

Brick also treats rental homes strictly. Owners must register the landlord with the clerk, apply for a Rental Certificate of Occupancy, and file a mercantile license with proof of at least $500,000 in liability coverage. Code Enforcement then inspects every rental each year, at $100 per inspection and $50 per failed re-inspection. The annual checklist covers smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, ground-fault outlets near water, a mounted fire extinguisher, and lead-safe status for structures built before 1978. Since September 27, 2022, creditors must also register foreclosed or vacant residential and commercial properties with the township within 10 days of filing a foreclosure action.

sections.h2: How are Brick property taxes billed, and what happens at closing?
sections.html:
Brick's tax year follows the calendar, with installments falling on the first of February, May, August and November and a ten-day grace window after each. Each bill covers a calendar quarter (the February bill pays for January through March), which matters at closing because the seller owes tax only through the closing date. A missing bill is no defense against interest, the tax collector warns, so make sure the closing agent has the current quarter's figure.

Work done on the house can add a second layer. After construction is finished, the township places an assessment on the improvement and mails an Added Assessment Bill in October, due November 1 and again on February 1 and May 1 of the following year. A seller who finished a deck or addition should ask the assessor whether that bill is still coming.

  • Assessment notices go out each year, usually by February 1, and an owner who thinks the value is wrong may appeal on or before April 1 to the Ocean County Board of Taxation.
  • Properties assessed above $1,000,000 can file directly with the State Tax Court of New Jersey.
  • The assessor processes veteran and senior or disabled deductions, each currently $250.

sections.h2: What does New Jersey charge a seller on a house sale?
sections.html:
The state's Realty Transfer Fee is the seller's cost, collected as the deed goes on record. On a standard sale of $350,000 or less, the rate is $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, $3.35 on the next $50,000, and $3.90 on the remainder. Above $350,000 the schedule starts at $2.90 and climbs to $4.80 per $500 between $200,000 and $550,000. At Brick's median value of roughly $410,600, most sales land in that second schedule. For the exact figure on your price, use the Division of Taxation rate tables.

Closing costs also include deed recording, any payoff of liens, and whatever the buyer negotiates for repairs. A cash buyer typically absorbs repairs, so the realistic comparison is your net after repairs, carrying costs through the winter, and agent fees against a single offer with a closing date you choose.

sections.h2: Is a cash sale the right call for a Brick homeowner?
sections.html:
A cash sale fits best when the home has defects an inspector would flag, when flood or storm damage is unrepaired, when the owner has inherited a house in another town, or when quarterly tax bills and a mortgage are piling up. It also helps landlords who do not want to carry the annual rental inspection cycle. It makes less sense for a move-in-ready home on a good street where a listing will draw several offers.

Whatever the buyer, get the offer on paper, set it beside the proceeds of a listing after commission, and confirm who pays for the certificate and recording steps. If you are close to a foreclosure filing, speak to a housing counselor or attorney in addition to any buyer, because the township's vacant property registration and the lender's timeline both affect your options.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Brick house if it was damaged in a storm?
faqs.a: Yes. Houses with storm damage change hands regularly, mostly to investors and cash buyers who subtract the repair bill. Collect your elevation certificate, flood claim paperwork and permit history first. The engineering office can look up certificates by address or by block and lot.

faqs.q: Which Brick office handles permits and certificates?
faqs.a: Start with the Division of Inspections voicemail line, 732-262-4604, or the permit status email on the township's building page. Rental certificate matters belong to Code Enforcement, 732-262-1033, weekdays.

faqs.q: What is the cutoff for contesting a Brick assessment?
faqs.a: April 1 each year, filed with the Ocean County Board of Taxation. Owners of property assessed above $1,000,000 may file directly with the State Tax Court of New Jersey instead.

faqs.q: Does a landlord need a certificate before selling a rented house in Brick?
faqs.a: A landlord needs the Rental Certificate of Occupancy to keep tenants in place, and the township inspects each rental every year. Ask the Division of Inspections what is required for your property when the sale closes and whether tenants move out first.

faqs.q: Who pays the realty transfer fee on a Brick sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays it. Recording the deed triggers the charge, which follows the price written in the deed and the Division of Taxation's published rates. Sales above $1,000,000 add a graduated percent fee.
